title: Ray Marching
description: March a ray through space and find where it hits a 3D shape.

lessons.title: Camera and ray setup
lessons.intro: Every shader up to here has answered a question about a point on a flat plane: given this coordinate, what colour? Ray marching asks something different. From an eye somewhere in space, looking out through this pixel, what is there? Answering that needs two vectors per pixel — where the ray starts, and which way it points — and building those is all this lesson does. There is no geometry yet and nothing to hit, so every stage paints the direction itself, which is the only honest way to check a camera before there is a scene to check it against.
lessons.takeaway: A camera is two vectors: an origin every pixel shares, and a direction that differs per pixel. The direction is the screen coordinate with a third component bolted on, and normalize scales it to unit length so that a distance travelled along it is a distance in the world. That third component is the field of view — raise it and the cone narrows, lower it and the cone widens — and the origin changes nothing you can see until there is something in front of it to miss.
lessons.tryThis: Set the focal length in the third stage to a fixed 0.4 and work out the colour at p of 1.0, 1.0 — on the top edge, one unit right of centre — before you look at it. Then change the 3.0 in the last stage's orbit radius and confirm that nothing on screen responds at all.

stages.title: One ray per pixel
stages.body: The first three lines are Module 1's, unchanged, but the preview they run on is a landscape band — between 1.4 and 2.4 times as wide as it is tall, depending on the screen. So p runs minus one to one vertically on every device, while the aspect line pushes it out to at least 1.4 either side horizontally, and further still on a wider screen. The two lines after that are the entire camera: every pixel shares one origin, and each gets its own direction, built by treating the screen coordinate as x and y and bolting 1.5 on as z. normalize scales that to unit length, which is what makes a distance travelled along it mean a distance in the world. Painting z alone shows the rays fanning out: 1.0 dead ahead, 0.832 one unit out in any direction — which is exactly the top and bottom edges — and lower still out toward the left and right, meeting 0.731 travelling straight out to the side edge of the narrowest phone and 0.530 on the widest — the frame's true minimum sits in the corners, lower again, since a corner pulls the ray off-axis on both screen axes at once. ro sits there unread, because nothing yet asks where a ray started.

stages.title: Paint the direction
stages.body: A unit vector has components between minus one and one, and half-plus-half lifts that into the 0 to 1 a colour needs — x into red, y into green, z into blue. The two screen axes behave quite differently here, because the frame is a landscape band, 1.4 to 2.4 times as wide as it is tall. Green is boxed in: 0.223 at the bottom edge, 0.777 at the top, and it can go no further, because p.y stops at one. Red passes through those same 0.223 and 0.777 one unit out and then keeps going to wherever the device puts the side edges — 0.841 at the right edge of the narrowest phone, 0.924 at the right edge of the widest. Blue is 1.0 dead ahead and 0.916 at the top and bottom edges, sagging further into the corners. What you get is a lavender band with red doing most of the travelling.

stages.title: The third component is the lens
stages.body: The 1.5 was never explained, and it is the field of view. A direction with a large z points more nearly straight ahead once normalized, so raising it narrows the cone the camera sees through and lowering it widens it. Here it swings between 0.6 and 2.4 every 12.6 seconds, which is a vertical field of view of 118.1 degrees at the wide end and 45.2 at the narrow, against 67.4 at the 1.5 the rest of the module uses — and the horizontal field is wider still, because the aspect scales the tangent of the half-angle rather than the angle itself. Watch a point away from the middle rather than the centre. At p of 1.0, 1.0, on the top edge and one unit right of centre, the colour runs from 0.825, 0.825, 0.695 wide open to 0.679, 0.679, 0.931 stopped down, while the centre pixel stays 0.5, 0.5, 1.0 throughout, because the ray straight ahead is the one the lens cannot tilt.

stages.title: Move the camera
stages.body: ro finally moves. It traces a circle of radius 3 about the point 3 units ahead, passing through the origin once every 15.7 seconds, and the direction is yawed by the same angle using Module 5's mat2 rotation applied to x and z instead of x and y — so the camera keeps looking at the centre of its own orbit. The centre pixel cycles through 0.5, 0.5, 1.0 then 0.0, 0.5, 0.5 then 0.5, 0.5, 0.0 then 1.0, 0.5, 0.5 at the quarter turns, which is the forward direction swinging all the way round. Change the orbit radius and nothing at all happens on screen. An origin is invisible until a ray hits something, and the next lesson builds the something.

lessons.title: A 3D sphere
lessons.intro: Module 3 built a circle out of length(p) minus a radius and never had to mention how many dimensions were involved, because length does not care. That is most of this lesson: hand the same expression a vec3 and it is a sphere. What genuinely changes is the viewing problem. A field defined throughout a volume cannot be shown all at once on a flat screen, so until the next lesson supplies a ray to look along, these stages cut one flat slice through the volume at a time and paint that slice as though it were the whole thing.
lessons.takeaway: length(p) minus r is a sphere for exactly the reason it was a circle: length measures distance from the origin in any number of dimensions, and subtracting a radius moves the zero surface out to where the edge should fall. Subtracting a centre first moves the sphere, and min unites two of them into one field. These are Module 3's operators carrying one more component, and the function that returns the whole scene's field is conventionally called map.

stages.title: One more component
stages.body: sdSphere is Module 3's circle with vec2 changed to vec3, and nothing else at all. The source builds a 3D point from the screen coordinate with a z of zero, which cuts the sphere through its equator, so the cross-section is a circle of the full radius 0.45 — forty-five per cent of the way to the top and bottom edges, and nowhere near the left and right, which sit at least 1.4 out even on the narrowest screen. The render is pixel-for-pixel a Module 3 disc, and that is the point: nothing has been gained yet except the knowledge that the formula survives the extra dimension. What has changed is that there is now a whole volume of field the screen is not showing you.

stages.title: Slide the slice
stages.body: Driving the slice's z from time cuts the same sphere at a different depth every frame, and the disc that comes back is the cross-section there. Its radius is 0.45 times the cosine of the driving angle: 0.45 at the equator, 0.390 once the slice reaches z 0.225, 0.270 at z 0.36, and zero at the poles — a pinch to nothing every 4.5 seconds, twice per nine-second cycle. That shrinking is the only evidence on screen that this is a sphere rather than a cylinder, and it is evidence you have to watch accumulate over time rather than read off any single frame.

stages.title: Move the sphere instead
stages.body: Subtracting a centre before measuring moves the sphere, exactly as it moved the circle two modules ago. The slice stays at z zero now and the sphere is what travels: a small circle of radius 0.1 in x and y every 10.5 seconds, and separately back and forth through the slice by 0.35 every 7.0 seconds. On screen those read as two unrelated effects — the disc slides about, and independently its radius breathes between 0.283 and 0.45. Both are one object moving. That a slide and a resize are indistinguishable in kind here is precisely the ambiguity a single slice cannot resolve, and the reason the next lesson stops slicing.

stages.title: Two spheres, one field
stages.body: map is the name this module and the three that follow use for the function returning the whole scene's distance, and here it is two spheres joined by min — Module 3's union, unchanged by the extra dimension. The two sit 0.44 apart in x and 0.3 apart in z, which is 0.533 in space, closer than the 0.68 sum of their radii, so they genuinely intersect. Watch them trade sizes as the slice sweeps: at z zero the left disc is 0.34 and the right 0.16, at z 0.15 both are 0.305, and at z 0.3 the sizes have swapped. Their centres are 0.44 apart on screen and the two radii sum to more than that at every one of those depths, so the outline stays a single joined shape throughout — they come apart only in a sliver around z minus 0.03, where the right disc has already shrunk under 0.101. It then vanishes altogether for about 46 per cent of the cycle, which is the slice leaving that sphere behind.

lessons.title: The march loop
lessons.intro: A slice shows one depth and has no room for the rest, and no amount of care choosing the depth fixes that. The way out is a different question. Send a ray from the camera through the pixel and ask how far it travels before it meets a surface. Nothing computes that distance directly, but a distance field answers something almost as useful at every point in space — how far you may move from here without hitting anything — and asking that question over and over is the entire algorithm.
lessons.takeaway: map returns the distance to the nearest surface, and that is by definition a distance the ray can travel safely. So march: step that far, resample, step again. The steps shrink as the surface approaches, so the ray converges on it and never passes through, while rays that miss take ever larger steps until they leave — which is why the loop needs a distance at which it gives up as well as a count of tries. More steps buy accuracy at the silhouette and almost nothing anywhere else.

stages.title: Step by the distance you have
stages.body: Four steps, written out rather than hidden inside a function. Each asks map how far the nearest surface is and moves exactly that far, which is safe precisely because nothing can be nearer than the nearest thing. The first step is identical for every pixel — map at the camera is 3 minus 1, so every ray leaps 2.0 — and only after that do they diverge. Painting the distance still remaining shows how far each one got: black across a core of radius 0.426, 0.051 out at the silhouette, 0.1 at radius 0.585, and not reaching white until 0.899. Past that it clips, and on a frame this wide more than half the picture is past that: 1.47 at one unit out, about 3.5 at the side edges on the narrowest phone, and about 7.5 on the widest. Four steps is already most of the way in.

stages.title: Enough steps, and a test
stages.body: Sixty-four steps in a loop, with two ways out: the distance dropping below 0.001, which means the ray has arrived, and the total passing 20, which means it never will. The sphere sits 3 units ahead with radius 1, so the tangent ray leaves the camera at asin of one third, 19.47 degrees; multiplying its tangent by the focal length of 1.5 predicts a silhouette of radius 0.530. What renders is 0.533, and since p.y stops at one that is just over half the way to the top and bottom edges — a disc a little over half the frame's height, sitting well clear of the sides on a preview this wide. Every hit falls between t of 2.0 dead ahead and 2.828 at the rim, so 20 is a very generous place to give up.

stages.title: What the extra steps buy
stages.body: The same scene marched twice, once with the full sixty-four steps and once with twelve, painted so that the disagreement is what you see: cyan where both find the sphere, coral where only the twelve-step march claims to. The coral is a ring from radius 0.533 out to 0.669 — twenty-five per cent too wide, a band 0.135 across in p units wrapped all the way round a disc whose true radius is 0.530. Of the rays that genuinely hit, 85.5 per cent converge inside twelve steps: pixels are area rather than radius, so the figure is the square of the radius ratio and not the ratio itself, and every failure lives in the outer annulus where the steps become tiny. Why the error goes outward rather than inward is the whole of the next lesson.

stages.title: Why it is called sphere tracing
stages.body: Each pixel here is the safe distance at the point its own ray has reached, squashed through d over one plus d so that it stays on screen. float(i) casts the loop counter so it can be compared against a step count that sweeps one to eight and restarts every 7.5 seconds — each count holding 0.83 seconds except the last, which holds 1.67 because the loop's ceiling of eight catches the top of the sweep. A count of zero would be a flat 0.667 everywhere, since map at the camera is 2.0 for every pixel, but the sweep crosses zero in an instant and no frame shows it. Watch the black core spread instead: 0.087, 0.255, 0.362, 0.426, 0.465, 0.489, 0.505, 0.515. One unit out the value dips once and then climbs away, 0.424, 0.405, 0.474, 0.595, 0.729, 0.839, 0.912, 0.954: the second step lands just past that ray's closest approach to the sphere, so it reads lower than the first, and from there every step carries it further out. That brightness is the radius of a ball around the ray guaranteed to be empty, and stepping across it is what gives the technique its other name.

lessons.title: The hit test
lessons.intro: Three numbers went into the last lesson's loop without an argument for any of them: the distance below which it declares a hit, the number of iterations it may spend, and the distance at which it concludes the ray has escaped. None of the three is a property of the sphere. All three are decisions about how much you are willing to spend and how much error you are prepared to accept, and every one of them shows up in the render when it is set wrong. Each stage here moves one of them and measures the damage.
lessons.takeaway: The threshold decides how near counts as touching, and because raising it lets grazing rays stop against a wider band of surface, it swells the silhouette rather than softening it. The step ceiling decides how long the loop may creep, and when it runs out the t it returns is neither a hit nor a miss — so a loop that can exhaust should say so rather than let the caller guess from t alone. The far distance decides where space stops, and set too near it cuts the scene instead of the background.

stages.title: How near counts as a hit
stages.body: The threshold is an argument now, swinging from 0.001 to 0.351 and back every 10.5 seconds. A ray stops as soon as the surface is within it, so what it really stops against is a sphere of radius one plus the threshold, and 1.5 times the tangent of asin of that over 3 predicts a disc growing from 0.531 to 0.757. The render gives 0.533 to 0.749, the shortfall at the loose end being big steps skipping straight past the thin shell. That is forty per cent wider in radius: the disc goes from reaching 53 per cent of the way to the top and bottom edges to reaching 75, on a shape that has not moved and a camera that has not turned.

stages.title: When the loop runs out
stages.body: Twelve steps, and the loop now says which way it ended: it returns the distance when it converged, and the negation of that distance when it gave up. Painting both readings apart is unkind to the usual test. Cyan marks where the march actually reached the surface, out to radius 0.490. Coral is everything the plain t-under-20 test would have called a hit as well, out to 0.669. The true silhouette is 0.530 and sits inside the coral band — the honest test falls 0.040 short, the loose one runs 0.138 long. Raise the ceiling back to sixty-four and the loose test's error drops to 0.003, which is why the previous lesson got away with it.

stages.title: Where space stops
stages.body: The far distance is the one that looks like a background control and is not. It swings between 1.6 and 3.2 here, and because the nearest point of the sphere sits at t of 2.0, anything below 2.0 empties the screen completely — a third of the cycle, about 4.2 seconds of nothing at all. Above it the disc grows back through 0.191 at 2.05, 0.359 at 2.2, 0.463 at 2.4 and 0.514 at 2.6, reaching its full 0.531 at 2.828, which is the distance to the rim. Beyond that it buys nothing: 3.2 gives 0.533. A far distance inside your scene does not trim the background, it removes scene.

stages.title: All three, set badly
stages.body: A threshold of 0.3, six steps and a far distance of 2.4, marched alongside a correct sixty-four-step march so that the difference is on screen: cyan where the good one hits, coral where only the broken one does. The coral reaches radius 0.639, twenty per cent too wide — a band 0.106 across in p units laid all the way round the correct silhouette. The worse damage is invisible here. Since map at the camera is 2.0 for every pixel, and the second sample is already under 0.3 anywhere inside radius 0.532, every ray on the face of the sphere returns t of exactly 2.0 — a constant. The depth is gone, which matters because the next lesson reads nothing but t.

lessons.title: Depth
lessons.intro: Every march so far has thrown away almost everything it worked out. The loop returns t, the distance the ray travelled before stopping, and each shader has asked exactly one question of it: is that small enough to count as a hit? But t is depth. It says how far away the surface is at this pixel, in the same units the scene itself is built in, and it is already sitting in a variable that cost nothing extra to fill. This lesson spends it four ways, and the first two are worth doing mostly for what they expose.
lessons.takeaway: t is a depth buffer you already own. Painting it raw is useless, because its range has nothing to do with 0 to 1 and has to be remapped by hand. Even remapped it makes a poor shading cue: on a sphere, depth changes slowly across the face and violently at the rim, so any ramp piles up in the outermost tenth of the radius. Where depth earns its keep is as a mask, and as the scalar behind a palette.

stages.title: Paint t and see almost nothing
stages.body: Dividing t by 20 and painting it grey is the naive move, and it is worth watching it fail. The background is pure white, because a ray that escapes returns something at or above 20 and the division cannot bring that under one. The sphere is a near-black disc: 0.100 dead ahead, 0.107 at radius 0.3, 0.126 at 0.5, and 0.139 at the rim. That is the entire shape rendered inside a band 0.039 wide out of a possible 1.0. The depth is real and it is correct — it is simply measured in world units, and nothing about world units maps onto a colour channel.

stages.title: Near and far as colour
stages.body: Two colours and a smoothstep from 1.2 to 3.7 turn depth into something readable, and the camera slides along z by 0.8 either way so there is a range to read — the first time moving ro has changed a single pixel. At its nearest the sphere is 2.2 away: the disc swells to radius 0.766, three-quarters of the way to the top and bottom edges, and the mix never rises above 0.221, so it reads as the near colour throughout. At its furthest, 3.8, it shrinks to 0.409 and the mix runs 0.705 to 0.999 — the rim lands on the far colour exactly, but the pole only reaches 0.422, 0.429, 0.512, whose red is still more than twice the far colour's 0.18. Across one sphere the effect is far weaker: at the middle position the mix runs 0.242 at the pole, 0.296 halfway out, 0.477 at 88 per cent and 0.720 at the rim, so just over half the swing hides in the outer eighth of the radius.

stages.title: Depth as a mask
stages.body: One comparison turns depth into a one-bit signal, and Module 7 spent a lesson on what one-bit signals are for. Here it composites the sphere over a sky built from the ray direction's y — a gradient spanning only 0.223 at the bottom of the frame to 0.777 at the top, because rd.y never reaches further than that, so its ends read 0.079, 0.132, 0.185 and 0.151, 0.338, 0.445 rather than the two colours in full. Those extremes sit on the vertical centre line: one unit out along the top edge the factor has already fallen to 0.743, and it keeps falling all the way to the corner, so on a frame this wide the bands bow rather than run straight. The disc is flat cyan at radius 0.533 with a hard edge, because a mask carries no shading whatever. What it does carry is a shape sitting over a background the very same rays produced.

stages.title: Depth into a palette
stages.body: Module 4's cosine palette takes any scalar at all, and t is a scalar. With c at 2.0 the depth range across the disc, 2.0 to 2.828, covers 1.66 cycles, and the drifting phase turns the whole thing over every 12.5 seconds. The bands are wildly uneven, and that is the finding rather than a flaw: measured outward from the centre, successive quarter-cycles land at 0, 55.0, 73.8, 85.5, 93.0, 97.5 and 99.6 per cent of the radius. Depth barely changes across the face of a sphere and then changes all at once at the rim, and a palette shows that in a way the grey ramp two stages ago could not.
